newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek police stop farmers from seizing toll booths.
newsitem.headline: Greek police stop farmers from seizing toll booths.

text.p: Riot police stopped farmers from occupying road toll booths in northern Greece on Friday to press their economic demands but there were no clashes, witnesses said.

Hundreds of farmers, demanding cheaper fuel and equipment and bigger state subsidies, tried to take over the booths in the northern Tempi and Moschohori areas aiming to prevent the state from collecting fees from drivers.
They were met by police and a public prosecutor who warned them that police would take action if they broke the law.
Traffic was halted for about an hour at the Tempi toll station because of the stand-off and the farmers eventually pulled back.
"The government is showing its true face. The police has orders to hit the farmers, to terrorise them. Our struggle will continue," farmers' representative Yannis Pattakis told reporters.
Farmers have vowed to block national roads next week despite government threats to arrest them if they carry out the protests.
"Next week the tractors will be on the highways and nothing will stop them." Thanasis Nasikas, another farmers' leader said.
Farmers blockaded roads for 25 days in December and vowed to do the same starting next Tuesday if their demands were not met.
They kicked off their action this week with demonstrations in major farm towns and a brief occupation of the main north-south railway on Thursday.
But Prime Minister Costas Simitis has pledged to keep the roads clear this time.
"Blocking the roads and not allowing citizens to move freely is unacceptable," he told parliament.
Government officials said hundreds of riot police units were on standby near the cenrtral towns of Karditsa and Larissa, headquarters of the farmers' protest.
Simitis has made minimal concessions to the farmers, saying his government cannot alter the European Union's farm policy or risk Greece's economic future to satisfy a single group.

The farmers are demanding lower fuel costs, cuts in value added tax on farm equipment, higher price supports -- especially for cotton -- and a $1.3 billion rescheduling of debts to the state Agricultural Bank.
